wound_authority: Pre-Brady non-disclosure doctrine; Mooney-Pyle-Napue line (1935-1959) — prohibiting false evidence only, not requiring disclosure of favorable evidence
jurisdiction: Federal constitutional — applicable in all states via Fourteenth Amendment
in_force_period: From the inception of federal constitutional due process doctrine until May 13, 1963
superseded_by: Brady v. Maryland, 373 U.S. 83 (1963); extended by Giglio v. United States, 405 U.S. 150 (1972); United States v. Agurs, 427 U.S. 97 (1976); United States v. Bagley, 473 U.S. 667 (1985)
current_status: SUPERSEDED — no operative legal effect. Brady and its progeny govern all criminal prosecutions in the United States.

primary_sources.holding: Conviction obtained through knowing use of perjured testimony violates due process — but no affirmative disclosure obligation announced
Reaffirmed Mooney — prosecution cannot use evidence known to be false
Prosecution cannot allow known false testimony to stand uncorrected — still no affirmative disclosure obligation

purpose_of_preservation: Defensive historical record — accurate citation of the pre-Brady legal gap that Brady v. Maryland closed. Documents the specific constitutional baseline from which Brady's reform was measured.
filed_by: Claude (assistant) under steward direction — Michael Hartmann
